pdef: A medication of the tricyclic antidepressant class, typically used in the treatment of major depressive disorder.
sdef: In pharmacological contexts, a therapeutic agent prescribed for its sedative and mood-elevating properties.

quotes.author: Dr. Robert Smith
quotes.sentence: The patient was prescribed **surmontil** to alleviate her depressive symptoms.

quotes.author: Jane Doe
quotes.sentence: After trying several medications, I found that **surmontil** worked best for my sleep patterns.

quotes.author: Dr. Sarah Jenkins
quotes.sentence: Caution is advised when prescribing **surmontil** to elderly patients due to its potential side effects.

pdef: A cold, dry wind blowing from the north or northeast across the mountains in the western Mediterranean.
sdef: A regional meteorological phenomenon characteristic of the coastal regions of Spain, France, and Italy.

quotes.author: Ernest Hemingway
quotes.sentence: The wind had shifted in the night and now the **tramontana** blew cold and clear.

quotes.author: Gabriel García Márquez
quotes.sentence: We were warned about the **tramontana**, a wind that drives people to madness.

quotes.author: Isabella Stewart
quotes.sentence: Sailing conditions became perilous when the sudden **tramontana** struck the bay.

pdef: Being or coming from the other side of the mountains, especially from beyond the Alps.
sdef: A person who lives beyond the mountains; occasionally used to denote someone perceived as foreign or barbarous.

quotes.author: John Ruskin
quotes.sentence: The architectural styles were heavily influenced by **tramontane** builders from the north.

quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle
quotes.sentence: He viewed the incoming forces as nothing more than **tramontane** invaders.

quotes.author: Lord Byron
quotes.sentence: I found the customs of these **tramontane** people to be starkly different from our own.

pdef: Situated on or originating from the other side of a mountain range.
sdef: Relating to regions or peoples located beyond a mountainous barrier, often used interchangeably with tramontane.

quotes.author: Wallace Stegner
quotes.sentence: The expedition mapped the vast **transmontane** territories that had never been surveyed.

quotes.author: Francis Parkman
quotes.sentence: They faced the daunting task of establishing a settlement in the **transmontane** wilderness.

quotes.author: Frederick Jackson Turner
quotes.sentence: Trade routes were established to connect the coastal cities with the **transmontane** settlements.

pdef: Advocating supreme papal authority in matters of faith and discipline.
sdef: Located south of the Alps, or originating from beyond the mountains, depending on the speaker's perspective.

quotes.author: Lytton Strachey
quotes.sentence: His religious views were decidedly **ultramontane**, placing absolute faith in Rome.

quotes.author: Thomas Macaulay
quotes.sentence: The political landscape was divided between nationalist factions and the **ultramontane** party.

quotes.author: John Henry Newman
quotes.sentence: I found myself increasingly sympathetic to the **ultramontane** arguments regarding church authority.

pdef: A clerical political conception within the Catholic Church that places strong emphasis on the prerogatives and powers of the Pope.
sdef: The doctrine or policy of advocating absolute papal supremacy, often historically opposed by Gallicanism.

quotes.author: Lord Acton
quotes.sentence: The rise of **ultramontanism** profoundly altered the balance of power within the church.

quotes.author: Owen Chadwick
quotes.sentence: Many secular leaders viewed **ultramontanism** as a direct threat to their national sovereignty.

quotes.author: Arthur Penrhyn Stanley
quotes.work: Lectures on the History of the Eastern Church
quotes.sentence: The council's declarations were seen as a definitive triumph for **ultramontanism**.

pdef: Not ordinarily encountered or experienced; out of the ordinary or unusual.
sdef: Remarkable or exceptional in amount, degree, or quality, standing out from the typical.

quotes.author: Jane Austen
quotes.sentence: She possessed an **uncommon** intelligence that set her apart from her peers.

quotes.author: Charles Dickens
quotes.sentence: It was an **uncommon** cold day, even for that time of year in the marshes.

quotes.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
quotes.sentence: The nature of this mystery is quite **uncommon**, Watson.

pdef: In a manner that is out of the ordinary; to a remarkable or exceptional degree.
sdef: Serving to emphasize an unusual quality, whether positive or negative, in a person or situation.

quotes.author: Charlotte Brontë
quotes.sentence: Mr. Rochester was in an **uncommonly** good mood that evening.

quotes.author: Herman Melville
quotes.sentence: The sea was **uncommonly** calm, belying the dangers that lurked beneath.

quotes.author: Mark Twain
quotes.sentence: Tom felt **uncommonly** proud of his cunning achievement with the whitewash.

pdef: The state or quality of being rare, unusual, or not frequently encountered.
sdef: The characteristic of being exceptional or remarkable, often conferring a special value.

quotes.author: Henry James
quotes.sentence: The sheer **uncommonness** of her beauty captivated everyone in the room.

quotes.author: Virginia Woolf
quotes.sentence: She cherished the **uncommonness** of a quiet moment in the bustling city.

quotes.author: George Eliot
quotes.sentence: The **uncommonness** of his intellect made him a difficult companion for ordinary folks.

pdef: Not tending to express feelings, especially of affection, openly or outwardly.
sdef: Characterized by a reserved or restrained emotional demeanor; lacking in expressive display.

quotes.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
quotes.sentence: His **undemonstrative** nature made it hard to tell if he was pleased or annoyed.

quotes.author: Agatha Christie
quotes.sentence: She was an **undemonstrative** woman, rarely showing any sign of panic.

quotes.author: Thomas Hardy
quotes.sentence: Oak remained calm and **undemonstrative**, accepting his fate without a word.
